strengths: The core idea of building a learnable memory of symbolic subroutines mined via LLM inductive reasoning from past successful toolpaths, combined with a fast-slow (subroutine-first, A* fallback) execution strategy, is sensible and well-motivated, and improves upon the authors' prior CoSTA* framework in a natural way.

The evaluation covers several axes: human-eval quality on a multi-turn image editing benchmark, execution cost, cost-quality Pareto analysis across alpha settings, ablations on subroutine verification, fast-only vs. slow-only variants, and a qualitative transfer test on MagicBrush tasks.

The subroutine verification loop (propose -> validate on subtask-specific test sets -> net-benefit acceptance -> retry) is a thoughtful mechanism, and the ablation (Table 4: fallback rate 28% vs. 9%) shows it matters.

The paper is generally well organized, with detailed appendices covering the learning loop, trace format, full learned rule table, prompts, and algorithms, which supports reproducibility of the methodology.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work: FaSTA* is a direct increment on the authors' own CoSTA* (arXiv 2503.10613), and the subroutine memory is essentially skill/rule caching of successful tool sequences, closely related to existing skill-library and experience-reuse ideas in LLM agents (e.g., Voyager-style skill learning, ICRL). The learned library ultimately contains only 16 subroutines across 5 subtask types, which limits the depth of the contribution.

The headline 49.3% cost saving appears confounded: the authors themselves show (Table 6) that simply changing the subtask prompt from multi-path tree to single chain reduces CoSTA* cost from 58.2s to 46.8s. The claimed saving should be reported against this improved baseline (implying ~37% rather than 49.3%), and the main-text comparison to 58.2s-like numbers overstates the benefit attributable to subroutine reuse.

Quality evaluation relies on human scores with no reported details on number of evaluators, inter-rater agreement, variance, or statistical significance; the benchmark is small (121 tasks) and inherited from the authors' prior paper, and the 3.2% quality drop is claimed without uncertainty analysis.

Potential evaluation leakage: the subtask-specific datasets used for subroutine verification are constructed from the CoSTA* benchmark images (Appendix J), and the final evaluation is on the same benchmark, so the learned/validated rule table may be tuned toward the evaluation distribution; the MagicBrush generalization evidence is only qualitative (a handful of examples).

Cost accounting is incomplete: the reported execution-time savings do not clearly include the overhead of the subroutine induction/refinement loop (periodic o1 calls, validation runs of baseline and candidate systems on sampled test sets), which could be substantial and should be amortized into the reported efficiency gains.

Heavy dependence on frontier proprietary models (GPT-4o, o1) and VLM quality checks; no mention of code or data release, weakening reproducibility of this largely empirical, prompt-engineering-heavy system.

Writing/care issues that undermine confidence: a spurious phrase ('Bi-Directional Block Self-Attention for Fast and Memory-Efficient Sequence Modeling') is clearly erroneously inserted mid-sentence in Section 4.3; references [9]/[10] and [18]/[19] are duplicates; several figures/plots are hard to read.
The empirical scope is narrow (one benchmark, one domain), so the claimed generality of the fast-slow neurosymbolic agent design beyond image editing remains untested.

strengths: The core engineering idea is sensible and clearly motivated: caching successful tool sequences as symbolic subroutines with activation rules, and only falling back to expensive A* search when fast planning fails, is a natural way to amortize exploration cost across tasks.

The system is described in reasonable depth: the subroutine induction loop (logging, periodic refinement, LLM proposal, verification with a Net-Benefit criterion), the fast-slow execution algorithm, and complete prompts and rule tables are provided in the appendix, which aids reproducibility of the pipeline.

The ablation studies (with vs. without subroutine verification; fast-only vs. full system vs. slow-only) are informative and support the claimed importance of each component, e.g., fallback rate dropping from 28% to 9% with verification.
An attempt is made to separate 'training' tasks from the benchmark during subroutine mining, and there is a small qualitative generalization check on MagicBrush tasks.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The central contribution — reusing previously successful plans/subroutines for future tasks — closely mirrors well-known ideas such as skill libraries (e.g., Voyager), plan/skill memoization, and hierarchical fast-slow planning with fallbacks. The delta over CoSTA* is essentially an LLM-constructed rule table plus a fallback trigger; framing this as a 'novel ICRL' improvement is overstated, and the high-level design could plausibly be implemented as memoization without LLM inductive reasoning.

Concerns about evaluation leakage and contamination. Although induction is claimed to use held-out non-benchmark tasks, the subroutine verification datasets (Appendix J) are built from the same 121 base images as the evaluation benchmark, and the final rule table (Table 7) contains benchmark-relevant cost/quality statistics. Even with re-worded prompts, the rule selection and acceptance decisions are tuned against data drawn from the evaluation images, weakening claims of genuine generalization.

The headline quality comparison is weak. The 3.2% quality difference is measured by human evaluation with no reported details on the number of evaluators, their expertise, blinding, inter-annotator agreement, or statistical significance. Baseline numbers are copied from the CoSTA* paper rather than re-run under identical conditions, and the entire evaluation rests on a single small benchmark (121 tasks).

The cost comparison is confounded. A substantial fraction of the savings (58.2s -> 46.8s, Appendix E) comes merely from changing the subtask-tree prompt to a single-path chain, not from the proposed method; the paper's headline of '49.3% cost saving' is only partially attributable to subroutine mining. It is also unclear whether the reported execution time includes the LLM calls for subroutine selection, inductive reasoning, and the costly verification procedure (which repeatedly runs full baselines), making the efficiency accounting potentially incomplete.

Success is partly circular: subroutine acceptance, fast-plan validation, and 'quality' all rely on the same VLM quality checks, so a subroutine that games the VLM check could be accepted as beneficial while the human-evaluated quality drops — which is exactly the small quality degradation observed.

Writing and presentation issues undermine confidence: duplicated identical references ([9] and [10]); an apparent template/paste error in Section 4.3 ('Bi-Directional Block Self-Attention for Fast and Memory-Efficient Sequence Modeling activation rules' — an unrelated phrase inserted mid-sentence); typos ('experiements', 'before integrate it into R'); Figure 1's claim that fast-plan success 'increases exponentially' is unsupported and reads as an overclaim; 'Detect the bench' example is used inconsistently.

Generalization evidence is anecdotal: the MagicBrush appendix shows only a handful of cherry-picked qualitative examples with no quantitative success rate, cost, or comparison, and the paper itself concedes a cold-start limitation without quantifying it.

Scope is narrow: the method is evaluated only within one tool graph over a small fixed set of subtask types (largely object recoloration/removal/replacement and text edits), and it is unclear how the approach would behave with more diverse, compositional, or longer-horizon tasks where subroutine conditions may not transfer.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: mining reusable symbolic subroutines from past toolpaths via LLM inductive reasoning, and reusing them in a fast-slow planning hierarchy where expensive A* search is only triggered on fallback.

The proposed online learning loop (data logging -> periodic inductive reasoning -> verification with a Net Benefit criterion -> retry refinement) is thoughtfully designed, and the verification step is shown by ablation (Table 4) to substantially reduce low-level fallback (28% -> 9%).

Strong empirical efficiency gains: ~50% reduction in average execution time relative to CoSTA* with only ~3.2% quality degradation, supported by Pareto frontier analysis across trade-off coefficient alpha values.

Honest analysis of confounds: Appendix E separately quantifies the cost reduction attributable to the single-path subtask chain prompt versus the adaptive fast-slow strategy, and the limitations (cold start, dependence on LLM capabilities) are candidly discussed.
Extensive appendix detail (complete rule table, trace composition, verification datasets, full prompts and algorithms) supports reproducibility of the methodology.
Additional generalization evidence: qualitative transfer of learned subroutines to the MagicBrush dataset without A* fallback, using rules learned from non-benchmark data.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the system is a direct increment over CoSTA* (same benchmark, same tool graph, same A* machinery, same evaluation protocol), and the core mechanism — a growing library of reusable skills/subroutines with activation conditions — closely mirrors well-known ideas such as skill libraries (e.g., Voyager) and in-context RL, so the conceptual contribution is modest.

Evaluation is confined to a single small benchmark (121 tasks) released with the direct prior work; no new benchmark is introduced, and the MagicBrush generalization evidence is only qualitative with a handful of examples and no quantitative metrics.

Potential evaluation-fairness/contamination concern: subroutine verification datasets (Appendix J) are built from the same 121 CoSTA* benchmark base images, so the rule table is validated — and implicitly tuned — on images that overlap with the final test set, despite claims of held-out separation for the induction stage itself.

Headline cost-savings number may be inflated: the baseline CoSTA* cost drops from 58.2s to 46.8s with the new single-chain prompt (Table 6), so the fair apples-to-apples comparison yields roughly 37% savings (29.5s vs 46.8s), not the advertised 49.3%; additionally, execution-time figures are inconsistent across the paper (58.2/46.8 in Table 6 vs ~61-65s in Figure 3).

Quality evaluation relies on human scoring without reporting rater identity, number of annotators, inter-annotator agreement, or statistical significance; the 0.91 vs 0.94 difference on 121 tasks is small and could be within evaluation noise, and automated-metric validation is absent.

No variance reporting or repeated runs for cost measurements; LLM/VLM outputs are stochastic and the online learning process introduces additional nondeterminism, making single-run results hard to interpret.

The overhead of the online learning loop itself (running CoSTA* and candidate-rule FaSTA* on test samples every K tasks, LLM calls to o1 for induction) is not accounted for in the reported per-task cost, so end-to-end cost-efficiency is overstated.

Heavy dependence on strong proprietary models (GPT-4o for planning, o1 for induction) raises both cost and reproducibility concerns; no experiments with open or smaller models to assess robustness of the pipeline.

Sloppy presentation issues: duplicated references ([9]/[10] and [18]/[19] are the same works), a stray template artifact ('Project:' on the title page), and some confusing figure labeling (Figure 3 alpha-value association with bars) reduce polish.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: reducing the computational bottleneck of A* search in toolpath agents for multi-turn image editing, building on the recent CoSTA* framework.

The core idea of online inductive reasoning over execution traces to synthesize symbolic subroutine rules with activation conditions is sensible, interpretable, and goes beyond simple caching (supported by the direct-cache baseline comparison in Table 14 showing dramatically lower fallback rates).

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: main benchmark plus independent Complex-Edit benchmark, cost-quality Pareto analysis across multiple alpha settings, ablations on subroutine verification, fast-only vs slow-only variants, LLM size impact, and LLM overhead accounting (49.3% to ~45.2% amortized savings).
Verification/selection loop with a Net Benefit criterion and retry mechanism is a thoughtful safeguard against LLM-proposed rule degradation, backed by ablation (28% vs 9% fallback).
Good transparency: complete subroutine rule table, detailed prompts, algorithms, and failure/fallback statistics are provided in the appendix; code and data are released.
Fair-comparison appendix (Tables 10-11) restricting toolsets to match baselines helps attribute gains to the planning architecture rather than tool access.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: skill/subroutine libraries learned from experience are well established (e.g., Voyager-style skill libraries, ICRL, caching of successful tool traces), and 'fast-slow' planning is a fairly natural combination of LLM planning with a search fallback. The contribution is primarily an engineering integration on top of CoSTA* from the same research group.

The headline cost savings are partly confounded: changing CoSTA*'s subtask tree to a single-path chain alone reduces CoSTA* cost from 58.2s to 46.8s (Table 12), so a nontrivial portion of the reported 49.3% saving versus the original baseline stems from a prompt modification rather than subroutine mining; the FaSTA* improvement over the already-improved baseline (46.8s to 29.5s) is smaller.

Small evaluation scale: 121 tasks / 550 subtask turns, human evaluation with unknown number of evaluators (only variance 0.07 reported), and ~3.2% quality degradation relative to the SOTA baseline. Statistical significance of the quality differences is not addressed.

Scope is narrow: subroutines are mined only for a handful of multi-path subtask types (recoloration, removal, replacement, text editing) on a benchmark whose task distribution heavily overlaps with CoSTA*'s design; generalization evidence (MagicBrush, Complex-Edit subset) is mostly qualitative or on a small subset.

Heavy dependence on proprietary frontier models (GPT-4o, GPT-o1) and VLM-based quality checks throughout (subtask planning, subroutine selection, induction, validation) raises reproducibility and cost concerns, and VLM-judged quality could bias both execution and the subroutine acceptance criterion.

Some claims are overstated or imprecise: e.g., fast-plan success rate 'increases exponentially' with explored tasks, 'human-like' framing, and minor inconsistencies/typos (e.g., 'FaSTA* begins to outperform FaSTA*') that suggest limited polish.

Cold-start behavior and sensitivity to subroutine distribution shift are acknowledged but only briefly analyzed; the learning trajectory (Table 7) shows quality slightly degrading (0.93 to 0.91) as more subroutines are learned, which deserves more scrutiny.

strengths: The core idea—mining symbolic subroutine rules from past toolpaths via LLM inductive reasoning and reusing them in a fast-slow planning scheme—is sensible and well-motivated, and the empirical trade-off (49.3% cost reduction for 3.2% quality drop vs. CoSTA*) is a meaningful improvement over the direct baseline.

The method is carefully engineered: online induction with periodic refinement, hypothesis-then-verify acceptance (Net Benefit criterion with retries), and lazy A* fallback constitute a reasonably principled pipeline with interpretable outputs.

Good effort at fair evaluation: held-out 'training' tasks excluded from the benchmark, ablations on subroutine verification and fast-only/slow-only variants, restricted-toolset comparisons (Tables 10-11), direct-caching baseline comparison (Table 14), LLM-overhead cost analysis, and comparison with end-to-end models (Gemini 2.0, GPT-4o).
Extensive appendices (prompts, algorithms, rule tables, dataset construction, human-eval protocol) support reproducibility, and code/data are stated to be released.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the contribution is largely a memory/caching layer on top of CoSTA*; fast-slow (model-based fast path + search fallback) and skill/subroutine reuse are established ideas (e.g., hierarchical RL, skill libraries in Voyager/RoboAgent, LLM skill induction), and the paper does not clearly distinguish its inductive-rule mechanism from prior skill-library work beyond the image-editing context.

Scope is narrow and benchmark-dependent: the main evaluation uses a single small dataset of 121 tasks / 550 manipulations from the CoSTA* paper, and several components (e.g., the specific activation rules, subtask taxonomy) appear tightly tailored to this tool/subtask suite, raising questions about generalization beyond this ecosystem.

Potential evaluation contamination: the subtask-specific verification datasets (Appendix L) are built from the same 121 benchmark images used for final evaluation, and quality during verification relies on the same VLM checks used at execution; the separation between 'learning' and 'benchmark' data is asserted but not rigorously demonstrated.

Human evaluation details are thin: number of evaluators, their expertise, blinding, and how partial scores were adjudicated are not fully specified; several key comparisons (e.g., Table 15 vs. Gemini/GPT-4o) are on 'a few tasks' or small subsets, limiting statistical strength.

Reliance on proprietary LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-o1) for decomposition, subroutine selection, and induction makes behavior and cost sensitive to model versions, complicating reproducibility; the paper itself concedes dependence on evolving LLM capabilities.

Claims are occasionally overstated or imprecise: 'success rate increases exponentially' (Fig. 1) from five points, inconsistencies in reported numbers (e.g., cold-start quality 0.93 in Table 7 vs. 0.94 in Table 3), and typos/grammatical errors ('experiements', 'FaSTA* begins to outperform FaSTA*', 'Bi-Directional Block Self-Attention' apparently spliced into a sentence about activation rules) that suggest insufficient polish.

The learned rules (Table 13) are largely hand-tuned-looking qualitative conditions ('Not too small', 'not White<->Black') evaluated only in aggregate; no analysis of rule interpretability, rule failure modes at scale, or sensitivity to the LLM's rule-induction quality is provided beyond one small-LLM experiment.

strengths: Practical and clearly motivated contribution: reusing successful toolpaths as symbolic subroutines is a sensible way to cut the dominant A* search cost of CoSTA*, and the reported ~49% cost reduction with only ~3.2% quality drop is a meaningful, consistent result across both the CoSTA* benchmark and the independent Complex-Edit benchmark.

The online subroutine induction/refinement loop is well-specified: trace logging, periodic LLM-based rule proposal, and an explicit verification step with a Net Benefit acceptance criterion and retry mechanism are documented in detail (Appendices G, L), which supports reproducibility.

Good ablation coverage: subroutine verification (fallback 28%->9%), fast-only vs. slow-only vs. full system, impact of LLM size, comparison with a direct-caching baseline, and restricted-toolset fairness comparisons strengthen the empirical claims.

Learning curves (Figure 1, Figure 9, Table 7) convincingly show the intended fast-slow behavior: fast-plan success rises and cost falls with experience while quality stays stable, and the cold-start behavior gracefully degrades to CoSTA*-level performance.

The paper is largely transparent about confounds: the subtask-chain prompt change is isolated (Table 12), LLM token overhead is analyzed, and limitations (cold start, dependence on LLM capability) are acknowledged.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea — caching/memorizing successful tool sequences as reusable skills with activation conditions — is a natural extension of CoSTA* and is closely related to classical skill/option discovery and macros in planning. The LLM-based inductive rule extraction is a reasonable instantiation but the conceptual advance over simply 'cache successful paths with conditions' (analyzed in Appendix J.1) is moderate, and the claimed link to in-context RL is loose.

Evaluation scale and rigor are limited: the primary benchmark is the baseline's own 121-task dataset, and quality is assessed by human evaluation with undisclosed evaluator count, blinding, or relation to the authors; an inter-evaluator variance of 0.07 is reported without further validation. The 3.2% average quality drop hides a larger degradation on the hardest tasks (0.91 vs 0.95 for 7-8 subtask image-only tasks), which is downplayed.

Potential test contamination: the subroutine verification datasets (Appendix L) are constructed from the same 121 base benchmark images used for final evaluation, so the rule-acceptance process (B(delta)<0) is effectively tuned on data drawn from the test distribution, weakening generalization claims.

Headline numbers require careful reading: the 49.3% cost saving is partly attributable to the single-path chain prompt (58.2s -> 46.8s for CoSTA* itself, Table 12), and Table 3 baseline numbers are quoted from the CoSTA* paper rather than re-run under identical conditions; the Pareto analysis (Figure 5) also uses an axis with gaps that complicates interpretation.

Several technical choices are ad hoc and not justified: the Net Benefit criterion B(delta) = deltaC% - deltaQ% sums percentage cost and quality changes with no weighting or trade-off justification; activation rules are purely qualitative ('not too small', 'not too extreme') with no systematic study of rule granularity or failure modes of rule matching by the LLM.

Writing and presentation quality is below the bar for a top-tier venue in places: garbled text (e.g., 'Bi-Directional Block Self-Attention for Fast and Memory-Efficient Sequence Modeling activation rules' in Sec. 4.3 is clearly an accidental paste), a sentence claiming 'FaSTA* begins to outperform FaSTA*' (Appendix C.1), and repeated typos ('experiements') suggest insufficient polish.

Generalization evidence is thin: MagicBrush evaluation is qualitative only (5 cherry-picked examples in Figure 7), and the end-to-end model comparison (Table 15) is on an unspecified subset with no cost accounting, limiting how far the claims extend beyond the CoSTA* setting.
